name: Irish nationalism
summary: Irish nationalism holds that the people of Ireland have the right to govern Ireland as a sovereign state, and aims at a united island free of British rule. It runs through cultural nationalism (language, literature, Gaelic games), constitutional Home Rule politics, physical-force republicanism and a small socialist strand. Today it is pursued mainly by consent and referendum under the Good Friday Agreement.
scope: The mainstream tradition from O'Connell and Parnell through the Gaelic revival and the 1916 Proclamation to the modern constitutional united-Ireland movement. It excludes dissident groups rejecting the Good Friday Agreement and does not separately profile socialist republicanism. Most answers on economic and social issues are low-confidence inferences, because the tradition is defined by national questions.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Not a nationalist question as such; the tradition's social-welfare strands and the Proclamation's equal-opportunity language lean toward public provision, inferred only.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Never addressed directly; the Proclamation's equal rights and Connolly's socialist strand suggest mild support, inferred.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Land reform and tenant protection against landlords show nationalism distrusting unregulated markets, though it has no market doctrine.

public-ownership.rationale: Socialist republicans favoured it but constitutional and cultural nationalists did not; the tradition is split.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: No settled nationalist position; adherents range from socialist republicans to farmers and conservatives.

unions-good.rationale: Connolly's socialist republican strand and labour links were part of the movement, but not central to the whole.

property-fundamental.rationale: Land League struggles overrode landlord property claims, yet later nationalism created many small owners who defended property.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Economic regulation was not a nationalist concern; adherents are divided.

cut-welfare.rationale: The Proclamation promises to cherish all children equally, suggesting hostility to cutting welfare, inferred.

worker-ownership.rationale: Only the Connolly socialist strand held this; most nationalists did not.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Nationalists were historically targets of British coercion and surveillance, making acceptance of state surveillance unlikely.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Traditional, Catholic-influenced social conservatism makes legalisation unlikely, though modern nationalists are mixed; inferred.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: No documented position; adherents split between civil-liberty and anti-sectarian concerns.

strong-leader.rationale: The tradition stresses popular sovereignty and a republic with elected government, not rule by a bypassing leader.

state-harmful.rationale: Irish nationalism seeks a sovereign state of its own, so it does not regard the state as unnecessary.

limit-guns.rationale: Armed tradition coexists with modern constitutional politics; no stated position.

empower-police-military.rationale: Nationalists have been wary of British-controlled police but support an Irish state's forces; split.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Cultural Catholic conservatism makes support unlikely, but no formal stance; inferred.

decide-locally.rationale: Nationalism favours national self-government over local, though it opposes rule from London; no clear stance on subsidiarity.

rehabilitation.rationale: Not a nationalist question; no documented position.

traditional-family.rationale: Nationalism has historically been bound up with Catholic social values, though modern adherents vary.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Historically conservative Catholic links, but modern nationalist parties back it; genuinely split across eras.

abortion-legal.rationale: Catholic-linked tradition versus modern Sinn Féin and SDLP divisions; split among adherents.

more-religion-public.rationale: Catholic identity entwined with nationalism, but the Proclamation guarantees religious liberty and republicans were secular; split.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not an issue the tradition addressed.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Cultural nationalism built on language, literature, music and Gaelic games is a core strand of the tradition.

gradual-change.rationale: Constitutional Home Rule nationalism was gradualist, but physical-force republicans rejected it.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Not a historic nationalist concern; Irish nationalism was an emigration-country movement and is inferred only.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Nationalists sought sovereignty, yet used international and EU frameworks to pursue unity; split.

free-trade.rationale: Not a defining position; Griffith favoured protection while others did not.

nation-first.rationale: Sovereignty is central, yet the movement is not hostile to global cooperation per se; ambiguous.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Not addressed by the tradition; adherents are divided.

open-borders.rationale: The nation-state ideal and its own border question make open borders an unlikely goal; inferred.

limit-growth.rationale: No stated environmental position and no support for limits on growth in nationalist writings; inferred.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Nationalist writings centre on sovereignty and culture and make no claim about technology solving human problems, so no stance can be derived.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Ireland has long opposed nuclear power and nationalist parties share this; inferred from state practice.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Proclamation cites six armed attempts at independence and republicans held that force was needed to found the republic.

experts-over-public.rationale: Popular sovereignty is the core claim of nationalism, implying scepticism of rule by experts.

central-planning.rationale: Not nationalist doctrine; only a small socialist strand would entertain it.

socialized-markets.rationale: Only the Connolly strand addressed it; split.

land-value-tax.rationale: Land reform was central but nationalists sought peasant ownership, not a land tax; not a defining position.

basic-income.rationale: Neither the land-reform tradition nor the Proclamation discusses unconditional state payments, and adherents range from socialists to conservatives.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Arthur Griffith's economic nationalism favoured protection, though it is not universal in the tradition.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Not an agreed position; some economic nationalists favoured it.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Land reform from the Land League to the Wyndham Act aimed to turn tenants into owners, spreading small property.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Only a marginal socialist strand held this; the mainstream sought a national republic with an ordinary economy.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: No stated position; mainstream nationalism builds a conventional state.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognised wage and price bodies are not part of nationalist programmes, and the sources show no position either way.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Proclamation promises a government elected by the suffrages of men and women, incompatible with single-party rule.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The Proclamation declares a republic; constitutional Home Rulers accepted the Crown, but the mainstream is republican.

democracy-best.rationale: The Proclamation commits to popular sovereignty and suffrage for men and women, and modern nationalism works through elections.

direct-votes.rationale: Referendums are the agreed route to unity, but there is no general doctrine of direct legislation.

workers-councils.rationale: Only the socialist republican strand approached it; the mainstream sought a parliamentary republic.

right-to-secede.rationale: Nationalists claim the right of Ireland to leave the UK and of Northern Ireland to join the south, though it is a nation-based not a region-based claim.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Proclamation promises equal rights and the people's ownership of Ireland, rejecting natural rulers.

political-violence-never.rationale: Physical-force republicanism is central to the tradition even though constitutional nationalists rejected it.

war-builds-character.rationale: Pearse-style blood sacrifice rhetoric existed, but the mainstream does not endorse it generally.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees religious liberty, but nationalism was closely linked to Catholicism; split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The tradition included Catholic influence but did not demand scripture-based law; the 1798 republicans were secular.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Nationalism seeks a sovereign state with its own institutions, so private courts and defence are alien to it.

military-superiority.rationale: Ireland is a small state with military neutrality; nationalism did not aim at superiority over rivals.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Proclamation promises equality to all citizens and blames division on an alien government, and the 1798 founders united Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Only the Connolly strand held this; the mainstream sees national struggle as the driving force.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The Proclamation promises equal rights and opportunities, which is not outcomes; split.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not addressed directly; the tradition framed Irish land claims against landlord and colonial dispossession.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Not a defining position, though the tradition sees British rule as colonial; adherents are split.

civilizational-union.rationale: Cultural nationalism stressed Irish distinctiveness from England, not union with a civilisational bloc.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Nationalist rhetoric of sacrifice for the nation opposes valuing self-interest morally.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The tradition stresses sacrifice for the nation but also guarantees rights in the Proclamation; split.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The tradition's attachment to the Irish landscape is cultural, and the sources take no position on nature's value apart from humans.

limit-population.rationale: Catholic-linked tradition and emigration history make population limits unlikely; inferred.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: No such view in the tradition; romantic strands valued rural Gaelic life but not rejection of industry.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Nationalism is about national self-government and cultural continuity, and its sources do not argue for speeding up technological disruption.

human-enhancement.rationale: Bodily and mental enhancement is outside the concerns of any nationalist source consulted, so the answer is a neutral placeholder.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: The tradition predates the question, and nationalists' history of state surveillance gives no clear lead beyond a split among adherents.

restore-past-order.rationale: Cultural nationalists sought revival of Gaelic tradition, but the movement was also forward-looking republicanism; split.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Nationalists hold a firm principle of sovereignty but have often been pragmatic in method, from Home Rule to the Agreement, so adherents split.

direct-action.rationale: Land League and republican traditions used direct action, while constitutional nationalism used parliaments; split.

return-to-foraging.rationale: No such position is found anywhere in nationalism.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Only the socialist strand would endorse it.

production-for-use.rationale: Only the socialist strand would endorse it.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Only the socialist strand would endorse it; the mainstream did not.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Not part of the mainstream; the aim was a democratic republic.

collective-farming.rationale: Land reform sought individual peasant ownership, not collective farming.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Only socialist republicans held this view.

taxation-theft.rationale: Nationalism builds a sovereign taxing state; it does not treat taxation as theft.

harm-principle.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees civil liberty but no nationalist source states a limit on state restriction, so adherents are split.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Nationalism is built on national group rights to self-determination.

conscription.rationale: Irish nationalists mobilised against the 1918 conscription threat; it is a famous nationalist cause.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Nationalism values voting and national self-government over exit.

state-as-business.rationale: No such view in the tradition.

media-academia-power.rationale: The sources do not discuss universities or media as power centres, and the claim is not a nationalist theme.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The Proclamation and the 1798 tradition reject ethnic division, and nationalists were themselves subject to colonial racial stereotypes.

organic-representation.rationale: Nationalism has used parliamentary parties, not organic or corporate representation.

total-state.rationale: Nationalist liberties, religious and civil liberty in the Proclamation, are inconsistent with total state direction.

national-rebirth.rationale: Cultural revival and Pearse's rhetoric of national regeneration are part of the tradition, though not all strands.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Nationalism seeks reunification of Ireland, not expansion abroad.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Popular sovereignty is the opposite of rule by personal oaths.

bound-labor.rationale: Nationalists fought the landlord system and fought for tenants' fixity of tenure, not serfdom.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Cultural nationalists argued that Irish culture was suppressed by anglicisation, but they made no general claim about the politics of knowledge.

universal-morality.rationale: Not addressed; the Catholic strand would agree.

single-common-good.rationale: Nationalism appealed to one national interest against an alien government, but it also operated through competing parties, so adherents are split.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: No position on Israel in the sources; adherents split though many nationalists sympathise with Palestinians.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Irish citizenship is open to descendants and Northern residents may take Irish citizenship, as the Agreement recognises; adherents generally support diaspora ties.

revive-national-language.rationale: The Gaelic League sought revival of Irish and the 1937 constitution made it the first official language, though adherents are split on compulsion.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Only the socialist republican strand of Connolly pointed this way, and the mainstream did not address how companies are run.

school-vouchers.rationale: Catholic school tradition could support it, but no stated position.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy was never a nationalist question, and adherents range across the economic spectrum.

economic-freedom.rationale: Nationalists did not tie political liberty to economic freedom, and the land reform tradition limited landlord economic freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Nationalism worked through law and elected assemblies.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Proclamation asserts the right of the people of Ireland to the ownership of Ireland; self-determination is the founding claim.

force-without-un.rationale: Ireland's tradition favours UN-backed action and neutrality; inferred.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Not a nationalist theme, and Irish nationalism has a diaspora and emigrant outlook; inferred.

work-for-welfare.rationale: No stated position; leans against harsh conditionality, inferred.

class-collaboration.rationale: Cross-class national unity was the movement's strategy, though socialists dissented.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Cultural nationalism revered inherited language, literature and tradition.

dominated-front.rationale: Irish nationalists identified with anti-colonial movements, but a specific front against the West is not their programme.

workers-nation.rationale: The Irish labour tradition under Connolly organised nationally, but the point is not central to the mainstream.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Proclamation promised suffrage for men and women, but traditional Catholic roles shaped the movement.

ban-interest.rationale: No such position in the tradition.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees equal rights to all citizens.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy policy is not addressed by nationalism, and adherents are divided between development and environmental views.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Not addressed; cultural nationalism values Irish culture but not forced assimilation.

proportional-representation.rationale: Ireland uses PR-STV and nationalists in the north favoured it as a protection for minorities, inferred from state practice.

national-mission.rationale: Not a feature; Irish nationalism concerned national self-rule rather than exporting government.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The Proclamation promised votes to women, but no nationalist source states a view on structural male advantage, and adherents differ.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Nationalists attacked an alien government rather than domestic elites as such, and parties have disagreed about their own politicians.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The Proclamation's equal treatment of all children is incompatible with eugenics.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Northern nationalists seek legal accountability for state killings in the Troubles, though their view of their own forces differs; reasonably documented in Sinn Féin and SDLP positions.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Nationalism sought an active nation-state including land reform and welfare; inferred.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The Proclamation's equality principle is inconsistent with it.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Proclamation promises equal rights and opportunities to all citizens and cherishing all children equally.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Only the socialist strand would address it; the Connolly line favoured an Irish Workers' Republic.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Nationalists regard the plantation of Ireland as colonial settlement, though this is not what unionists say.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The Proclamation promises equal rights, but denominational influence on Irish law meant nationalists never took a settled position on uniform civil law.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not part of the tradition and contrary to its rural livestock economy.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Catholic-linked tradition generally accepts denominational schooling.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Only socialist republicanism would address it.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Proclamation and the Agreement alike rest on popular sovereignty and consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Griffith's economic nationalism valued home production, but a general export-surplus aim is not a stated nationalist position.

population-transfer.rationale: The Proclamation condemns division and promises equality to all; transfer is contrary to its stated principles.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Physical-force nationalists accepted initiating force, though constitutional nationalists did not; the tradition leans against an absolute ban.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Not nationalist doctrine; no documented position.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Nationalists were themselves banned or interned historically, and Sinn Féin was once banned from broadcasts; inferred opposition.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The independence claim is that rule by an alien government is domination regardless of how it is exercised.

vanguard-party.rationale: Only the IRB-style secret organisation approached it; mainstream nationalism is mass and electoral.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The Proclamation promises equal opportunities, and land reform helped tenant poor; inferred.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Nationalist land reform created owner-occupiers, extending to tenants buying their homes by analogy.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The movement's labour wing opposed it; inferred.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Nationalists blamed British land and famine policy, not population, for poverty.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Nationalists suffered coercion acts and internment; inferred opposition.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Famine-era grievances about food exports might favour it, but no nationalist source states a view on maximum prices.

party-controls-media.rationale: Inconsistent with civil liberty in the Proclamation.

party-commands-army.rationale: The IRA often acted independently of the Dáil, but the mainstream recognised state control of forces.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship waiting periods are not discussed in the tradition, which has focused on citizenship for people of Irish descent or birth.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Only some socialist republican voices raised it.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Nationalism values sovereignty, but Ireland uses EU membership; Sinn Féin has been Eurosceptic while others are pro-EU; split.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Irish tradition uses a parliamentary government with a largely ceremonial president.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Catholic-linked tradition, but not a political position.

clerical-rule.rationale: The hierarchy opposed violent republicanism and never held political rule.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Irish nationalists opposed participation in the First World War in the republican strand but constitutional Redmond backed it.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Cultural nationalists valued literature and the Celtic Revival; Irish censorship was a Catholic-state policy not nationalist doctrine.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Term limits are not a nationalist issue; the Proclamation promises an elected government but is silent on re-election.

recall-officials.rationale: Nationalists used elections and referendums, but the sources do not mention recalling officials.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Irish military neutrality is entrenched, and republicans oppose alliances such as NATO.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Land reform sought tenant purchase, not abolishing rented housing.

people-in-arms.rationale: Irish Volunteers and the Citizen Army were citizen armies that nationalists celebrate.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Gaelic revival romanticised rural, Irish-speaking communities.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Reunifying the island is the defining aim of Irish nationalism, now through consent referendums.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Many nationalist leaders were educated and middle-class, and the sources make no claim about graduates being out of touch.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Hyde's cultural nationalism asserted Irish distinctiveness against anglicisation and its equal worth.

death-penalty.rationale: Not addressed directly; Ireland abolished it, and nationalists were victims of executions after 1916.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Not a stated position; inferred opposition.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Catholic-influenced social conservatism might favour it, while civil-liberty nationalists would not, and no source settles it.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Irish citizenship passes through descent and the Agreement lets Northern residents be Irish; inferred from state practice.

minority-language-support.rationale: Irish is a minority language in the north and the Agreement commits to respect for Irish and Ulster Scots, which nationalists support.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees religious liberty but there is no exemption doctrine.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Cultural nationalists valued custom and community, but the sources do not take a position on social pressure and eccentricity.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Famine memory and anti-colonial identification could favour it, but no nationalist source states a view on sovereign debt.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Land reform and Connolly's argument tied independence to economic change, though mainstream views vary.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The Proclamation and the First Dáil appealed to an elected national assembly for the republic.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Nationalism rests on liberty as set out in the Proclamation.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Ireland's famine memory and anti-colonial identification support aid, inferred.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Ireland has no nuclear weapons and nationalists oppose them.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Ireland directly elects its president; the republic ideal supports it, inferred.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Monetary institutions were not a nationalist issue, and the sources give no position.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Nationalists claim the whole island but accepted the Agreement; split.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Land reform subordinated landlord rights to tenants' needs, supporting a social view of property.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The characterisation of the USSR is not addressed by Irish nationalism, and only a small socialist strand would have a view.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation was not part of nationalist programmes, and adherents are split.

collective-defense.rationale: Neutrality is entrenched in Ireland; the tradition is split on alliances.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Nationalists regard British rule in Ireland and the north as imposed without consent of the Irish people.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Catholic Church and nationalism were closely allied, so curbing clerical power was not mainstream.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Ireland's president is a non-partisan symbol and Hyde was the first; inferred.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Nationalists claim the right to break from UK; they do not support forcing regions to remain.

region-keeps-system.rationale: The Agreement and Northern autonomy arrangements show nationalists accept devolution inside a larger state; inferred.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The Proclamation is republican and rejects monarchy.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax structure was not a defining nationalist concern, and the sources show no position.

character-from-environment.rationale: Nationalists blamed British policy for Irish conditions, but the tradition has no theory of how character forms.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Popular sovereignty rejects rulers above the law.

space-expansion.rationale: A space programme is far from the concerns of national self-government and culture, so the sources give no position.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The Proclamation sets out a republic by popular suffrage, but a mix of few and many is not a nationalist doctrine.

leader-cult.rationale: Republican egalitarianism is wary of leader cults though martyrs are honoured.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family-court presumptions are not addressed in any nationalist source, and adherents are split.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The Proclamation blames division on an alien government and promises equality to all, so adherents do not see diversity as the cause of conflict; inferred.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Only the small socialist strand (Connolly) addresses this and the mainstream tradition does not; no settled position, inferred.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Land War and Land League campaigns transferred estates from landlords to tenant farmers, and the Proclamation asserts the people's ownership of Ireland.

refugee-return.rationale: Not a defining question; the tradition's emphasis on the people's right to their land suggests support for return, inferred.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Mainstream nationalism claims the island of Ireland as a territorial unit, not territory because of kin elsewhere, and now pursues unity only by consent under the Agreement.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees religious and civil liberty to all citizens, which excludes punishing a change of religion.

women-must-cover.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees equal rights and liberty; compulsory dress codes for women have no place in the tradition, inferred from that.

common-currency.rationale: Never addressed as a nationalist question; Irish nationalists are split between valuing sovereignty and backing EU integration, so left neutral.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-Celtic sentiment existed in the cultural revival but not as a political programme; the aim is an independent Irish state, inferred.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The tradition seeks a sovereign state for the Irish nation rather than minority cultural autonomy within British rule, though the Agreement protects cultural identity within Northern Ireland.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Nationalists in Northern Ireland pursued civil rights where they lived while also seeking unity; the statement does not map onto emigration, so left neutral.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Cultural and national revival (language, literature, identity) is central to the tradition, which treats ideas as drivers; only the socialist strand differs. Inferred.

ban-cartels.rationale: Not addressed; no settled nationalist view on competition policy.

no-bailouts.rationale: Not addressed by the tradition and adherents are split; left neutral.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The Proclamation and Agreement stress equal rights and protections for all, and the Agreement's rights provisions limit majorities; inferred.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The Proclamation promises equal rights and suffrage to men and women, but quotas are a modern policy not addressed by the tradition and views are split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Early 20th-century Sinn Fein advocated economic self-reliance, but the modern tradition is pro-EU; split between phases, so neutral.

moral-incentives.rationale: Not addressed; the mainstream tradition is not communist and does not pursue replacing material incentives, inferred.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The 1916 Rising was staged by a small armed group of the IRB and Volunteers to spark national revolt, and physical-force republicanism is a core strand, though the modern mainstream rejects violence.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees equal rights and opportunities to all citizens and the tradition is republican, so hereditary privilege has no place; inferred.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Cultural nationalism, led by the Gaelic League, put Irish language, literature and history at the centre of national identity.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The tradition is defined by rejecting British rule of Ireland, however justified, and the Proclamation asserts the right of the Irish people to govern themselves.

patriotic-education.rationale: Inferred from the cultural-nationalist revival and Irish-language schooling; patriotic loyalty in schools is not a core demand.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Inferred from the Proclamation guarantee of equal rights and equal opportunities to all citizens.

public-money-creation.rationale: Not a nationalist question; the tradition has no shared monetary doctrine.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Not addressed; inferred neutral because the tradition holds no common theory of capitalism.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Irish nationalism is anti-imperial in origin and opposes British influence; inferred to reject cultivating influence in a predecessor empire's lands.

delink-world-market.rationale: Early economic nationalism favoured protection, but the modern mainstream is not delinkist; adherents are split.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Not addressed by the tradition; only a small socialist strand has a view.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees equal rights and equal opportunities and religious liberty, which cuts against a free-to-discriminate stance.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Good Friday Agreement and the Proclamation both commit to protected rights and equality; entrenchment is inferred.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Inferred: partition was imposed by Westminster without the consent of the island as a whole, so nationalists deny its moral force.

elective-rulers.rationale: The 1916 Proclamation declares a republic with a government elected by the whole people, not a hereditary crown.

minority-veto.rationale: Inferred: nationalists reject a unionist veto over unity, accepting only the all-island consent principle of the Agreement.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Inferred from a tradition of resisting British rule as illegitimate and, in the republican strand, rebellion.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Proclamation places sovereignty in the people and their elected representatives, not a monarch.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Inferred: the tradition has no stated position on animals; a mainstream modern adherent would agree.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Inferred: no stated position; a rural, farming-rooted tradition accepts humane use.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Inferred: the Proclamation stresses equality of all children of the nation rather than paternalist duty, but charity is widely accepted.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Inferred: the movement is built on active political participation and mobilisation.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Inferred: cultural nationalists feared Anglicisation by mass culture, but the claim is a Marxist one and is not a stated position.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Inferred: not a theme of the tradition; adherents are split.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Inferred from the nationalist narrative of colonial economic exploitation under British rule.

native-born-offices.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees equal rights and opportunities to all citizens, which cuts against reserving offices by birth.

party-own-road.rationale: Inferred from the principle of national self-determination and the Sinn Fein motto of ourselves alone.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Inferred from the Sinn Fein tradition of national economic self-sufficiency; modern adherents accept EU funds.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Partition is not a loss in war, so the fit is loose; inferred from the central demand to end it and reunite the island.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Inferred: the Proclamation cherishes all the nation equally and the tradition seeks to unite Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Inferred: not addressed by the tradition; adherents are split.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Inferred: not addressed; mainstream adherents condemn both but the equivalence is contested.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Inferred: the tradition has no stake in the question and a mainstream adherent would accept the historical consensus.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Inferred: nationalists have removed or renamed symbols of British rule, such as Nelson Pillar.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Inferred: no stated position; a mainstream modern adherent would agree.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Inferred: not addressed; adherents are split.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Inferred: the tradition aims at a Western-style democratic republic.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Inferred: the modern constitutional movement stresses civilian democratic control and renounces force.

paid-care-work.rationale: Inferred: not addressed; adherents are split.

filial-duty.rationale: Inferred from the Catholic and rural social traditions of the movement; not a nationalist question.

office-by-exam.rationale: The Proclamation promises democratic government by the people's elected representatives; exams are not addressed. Inferred.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: The Proclamation claims 'the ownership of Ireland' for the Irish people, so national control of key assets is favoured; inferred.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Adherents split: older Catholic nationalism opposed divorce while modern constitutional nationalists accepted it.

recallable-delegates.rationale: The Good Friday Agreement settled on a regular elected assembly and fixed terms; recall of delegates is not part of the tradition.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the tradition's mainstream acceptance of mixed economies and private savings.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Land League nationalism sought peasant ownership of land, not common tenure, though the Proclamation claims land for the people; inferred.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Home Rule and Parnell's parliamentary movement aimed at an Irish parliament with control of its own finances.

single-official-language.rationale: The Gaelic League sought to revive Irish alongside English without banning other languages; inferred.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The Proclamation's claim that Ireland belongs to the Irish people and the Land War history suggest keeping land in native hands; inferred.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Not a nationalist question, and adherents have no shared view.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Not a nationalist question, and adherents have no shared view.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Mainstream constitutional nationalism renounces armed force and Ireland's neutrality counsels against arming foreign rebels; inferred.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: The tradition's own experience of rule from outside makes it hostile to forceful intervention; inferred.

corporate-influence.rationale: Not a nationalist question; the tradition has no shared position on lobbying or campaign finance.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Irish nationalism fought for sovereignty but has not addressed foreign funding of NGOs; diaspora funding was historically important to the movement.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Not addressed by the tradition; Catholic social teaching favors families, but no nationalist program states incentive policy.

residents-only-property.rationale: Land reform and tenant ownership against absentee landlords were central to the movement, so local ownership limits are a plausible fit; inferred.

job-guarantee.rationale: Not addressed; the tradition's social and socialist strands might support it but it is not a nationalist position.

democratic-peace.rationale: Not addressed by the tradition; Irish neutrality and anti-imperial history make adherents skeptical of democracy-promotion wars, but the claim itself is not engaged.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The tradition includes a founding tradition of rebellion against British law, but the modern constitutional strand accepts the rule of law; inferred.

non-intervention.rationale: Irish nationalism rejects British interference in Ireland but accepts international bodies and the Good Friday Agreement's external guarantees, so a flat ban is unlikely.

industrial-unions.rationale: Not addressed by the nationalist tradition; Irish labor history includes both craft and industrial unions.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees religious and civil liberty to all citizens, so a minority-conspiracy claim is not mainstream.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The tradition is strongly tied to Catholic family norms; modern strands have not sought to end legal marriage. Inferred.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The Proclamation's equal-rights language and the modern constitutional strand favor open government; inferred, not stated.

local-production.rationale: Cultural nationalism praised rural self-sufficiency, but there is no stated localism position on production.

informal-organisation.rationale: The mainstream tradition worked through parties and organizations (Home Rule, Sinn Fein, the Gaelic League), not small informal groups.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The modern movement accepts the Good Friday Agreement's international framework and treaty commitments, so it does not put national law above international law.

religious-nation.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees religious liberty and the Good Friday Agreement affirms parity of esteem; the mainstream nation is civic and cultural rather than defined by religion.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The tradition is defined by rejecting rule by a stronger neighbour, so ritual deference to a leading power is inferred to be rejected.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The Proclamation addresses the whole island as one, so pooling revenue across regions is inferred to be preferred.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The tradition has no settled view on common ownership; its land-reform and small-property strand suggests private possessions but not collective means.

defeat-communism.rationale: Catholic-leaning mainstream nationalism was historically hostile to communism; inferred from that, not a defining issue.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: No stated position; adherents divide between state and mixed provision.

religion-illusion.rationale: Strong Catholic tradition in the movement implies religion is held to answer lasting needs; inferred only.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The tradition did not address capitalism as a stage; adherents are split between its socialist strand and constitutional liberals.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Proclamation promises equal rights through the republic, so equality is framed as legal and political; inferred only.

socialized-care.rationale: Socially conservative, family-centred tradition inferred to prefer private care.

purge-loanwords.rationale: The Gaelic League sought to de-Anglicise Irish culture and revive the language, so purging English loans is inferred to fit, though it is not stated.

treaties-binding.rationale: The Good Friday Agreement is treated as a binding settlement among parties and governments; inferred to favour lasting treaties.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Mainstream nationalism seeks a unified sovereign state, not commune networks; inferred from the Proclamation.

majority-settlement.rationale: Nationalists claim equal rights for all communities on the island and would oppose majority-steering settlement; inferred from the Agreement and Proclamation.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The tradition is defined by national questions and has no stated third-way doctrine; adherents are split.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Inferred: the tradition grounds Irish sovereignty in the Irish people's long-standing nationhood, though it also accepts the consent of present residents under the Agreement.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; mainstream nationalism accepts the established historical record.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; modern constitutional nationalism supports equality, and Ireland decriminalised in 1993 and legalised marriage in 2015.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Inferred from the Proclamation's equal rights and the Agreement's democratic framework; the tradition itself suffered suppression by the British.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees religious and civil liberty and equal rights to all citizens.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Irish nationalism arose in opposition to British rule and its alien government, and the Proclamation asserts the people's ownership of the country.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; inferred as the tradition having no religious duty doctrine of this kind.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees religious liberty and rests authority on the Irish people, not on religious law.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Not a nationalist question; adherents have no shared view beyond representative democracy and referendums.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; the socialist strand would agree, other strands focus on the national question.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; adherents are split between modern liberal and traditional views.

assisted-dying.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; Catholic-influenced and liberal adherents are split.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The tradition is defined by the national question and spans left and right, so it neither affirms nor denies the divide.

alienated-labor.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; only the small socialist strand would agree.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; the Proclamation's equal rights and the Agreement's identity provisions suggest rejection, but adherents have no shared position.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Proclamation derives the Republic's authority from the Irish people and their right to ownership of Ireland, while invoking God only in passing.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; inferred from the Proclamation's religious liberty.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Not addressed in the sources, and the tradition has no position on employment contracts.

social-market-economy.rationale: Not a nationalist question as such; adherents range from the socialist strand to free-market supporters.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The tradition rests on physical-force republicanism and the 1916 Proclamation's call to arms, and an independent Ireland maintains defence forces.

rich-first.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; adherents range across the economic spectrum.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Inferred: independent Ireland's tradition of military neutrality is closely tied to national sovereignty, though the sources do not state it.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The 1916 Proclamation founds a republic, and Irish republicanism defines itself against hereditary monarchy.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: The tradition had cooperative credit movements, such as the Plunkett cooperatives and credit unions, but no stated doctrine; adherents are split.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Sovereignty from foreign control suggests suspicion of imposed terms, but the Irish state accepted the 2010 EU/IMF programme; the position is inferred.

property-franchise.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees universal suffrage by addressing Irishmen and Irishwomen and promises equal rights and opportunities to all citizens.

domination-women-nature.rationale: The Proclamation grants women equal citizenship, but no link to the domination of nature is stated in the tradition; inferred as split.

reification.rationale: This Marxist concept lies outside the mainstream tradition; inferred as indifferent.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The mainstream tradition values free press and assembly and accepts private media; inferred, with a socialist strand dissenting.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Constitutional nationalism from O'Connell onward argued within the law and the Agreement is a legal settlement; the physical-force strand did not; inferred.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees equal rights and equal opportunities to all citizens and declares itself for the whole people, not one group.

online-participation.rationale: The tradition has no stated position; adherents are split and the answer is inferred.

open-government-data.rationale: Mild support is inferred from the democratic republic described in the Proclamation; no stated position.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The Proclamation promises religious and civil liberty and cherishing all children equally, though Catholic social influence was strong; inferred.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The Proclamation pledges religious and civil liberty and equal rights, and the tradition formally rejects sectarianism despite the 1904 Limerick boycott; the position is the documented majority view.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Irish nationalists have backed citizens' assemblies, notably on a united Ireland and constitutional questions, and the Good Friday Agreement's consent model fits deliberative input; inferred, not a founding doctrine.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: The tradition is split between a Catholic-aligned strand and an anticlerical republican one, and it is defined by national questions; inferred.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Proclamation promises equal rights and opportunities for all citizens, from which concern about concentrated power and wealth is inferred.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Not addressed by the tradition; inferred from modern constitutional nationalism's liberal and equal-rights turn.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The tradition was closely tied to Catholic and Gaelic culture and the Agreement guarantees religious freedom; state-promoted atheism is inferred as strongly rejected.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Not addressed; the tradition seeks its own state with police and courts, so abolition is inferred as rejected.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The Good Friday Agreement set up mandatory power-sharing between nationalist and unionist communities, which constitutional nationalists accepted and championed.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Not addressed; the tradition has no stated view on charity against state aid.

vote-delegation.rationale: Not addressed; delegable voting is a modern idea outside the tradition.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Not addressed; outside the tradition's national concerns.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Adherents are split, with the Catholic tradition largely against and modern nationalists for; no common view.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Proclamation addresses men and women alike and promises equal rights, from which shared marital authority is inferred.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: The Good Friday Agreement era tradition stresses equal rights and inclusive citizenship, and Ireland allows resident non-citizens to vote locally; inferred as mild support.

rent-control.rationale: Housing policy is not a nationalist question, and adherents range from socialist to conservative, so no direction is stated.

abolish-ip.rationale: Never addressed; the cultural-nationalist tradition values authors' and artists' works, so abolition is inferred to be disfavoured.

uniformed-youth.rationale: The Gaelic League and Home Rule traditions were civic and cultural; drilled youth movements recalled Fianna Eireann in the republican strand only, and the mainstream today rejects national-service drilling.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Ireland has long had a neutrality and anti-nuclear stance not stated in the sources; inferred from that tradition.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: The tradition's core is ending foreign rule of Ireland, and independent Ireland kept neutrality and no foreign bases; inferred from sovereignty claims in the Proclamation.

recognise-genocide.rationale: The tradition recognises the Famine as a wrong done by Britain, though the sources do not discuss formal genocide recognition, so inferred.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The Proclamation promises equal opportunity and land reform was central to the movement, so income from labour over rents is inferred.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Irish nationalism includes a strong physical-force tradition from 1916 onward, and the Proclamation appeals to arms, so adherents do not hold killing in defence to be wrong.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The tradition roots the Irish nation in Gaelic and ancient origins and invokes that continuity in the revival and the Proclamation, though modern civic nationalism is more qualified.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Not a nationalist question; adherents are split and the sources are silent.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Not addressed by the tradition; adherents split, so inferred as neutral.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: The tradition honours the 1916 leaders and republican dead as martyrs, a central part of its commemorative culture, shown in the Proclamation's call to sacrifice.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The mainstream tradition is political and constitutional, and the Proclamation is secular in its guarantee of religious liberty, so politics is not framed as spiritual combat.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: The Gaelic revival held that Ireland's culture could be sustained worldwide among the Irish diaspora, and the Good Friday Agreement extends identity and citizenship beyond the state.

culture-before-state.rationale: The Gaelic League explicitly set out to revive language and culture as the foundation for independence, in the cultural nationalism that preceded the 1916 rising.

god-not-male.rationale: Not addressed by the national tradition; adherents are split between Catholic, Protestant and secular, so inferred as neutral.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Not addressed; adherents are split and the sources do not discuss it.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The Proclamation guarantees equal rights and equal opportunities to all citizens and cherishes all children of the nation equally, which rules out reserving economic life to a majority.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: The tradition seeks one island-wide state, not separate units for peoples, and the Good Friday Agreement keeps Northern Ireland's two communities within a shared structure; inferred.

missingStatements.text: A united Ireland should come about only if majorities in both parts of the island vote for it.
missingStatements.rationale: Modern constitutional nationalism accepts the consent principle and a referendum route to unity under the Agreement.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to the Northern Ireland settlement; consent-of-governed and national-self-determination cover the principle.

missingStatements.text: A people should be free to govern themselves and own their country's land and resources, free of rule by a foreign government.
missingStatements.rationale: The Proclamation asserts the people's ownership of Ireland and blames division on an alien government.

notes: Constitutional, republican, cultural and socialist strands answer differently on violence, religion and economics; neutral or low answers reflect that split.
